[QUERY] What brings you in today? Please describe your main symptom or concern, including when it started and how it has progressed.

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient reports exercising in the gym several hours ago when she suddenly felt a sharp pain in her lower back.  
[REFERENCE] 3. She describes the pain as radiating down the side of her leg and into her foot.  
[RESPONSE] I came in because I suddenly felt a sharp pain in my lower back while exercising at the gym several hours ago. The pain radiates down the side of my leg and into my foot.

[THOUGHT] The patient presents with acute-onset sharp lower back pain radiating down the lateral leg and into the foot — a classic radicular pattern. This strongly suggests lumbar nerve root irritation, most commonly due to a lumbar disc herniation (e.g., L4–L5 or L5–S1). Key next steps are to assess for red flags (e.g., cauda equina syndrome, infection, malignancy) and neurologic deficits. Since cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency, I must immediately screen for saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, or bilateral leg weakness — but the patient hasn’t reported these yet. Also, radiation to the lateral leg and foot points toward L5 or S1 involvement; confirming motor/sensory findings will help localize. First, I’ll ask about associated neurologic symptoms — specifically numbness/tingling distribution and any weakness — to narrow the level and assess severity.

[QUERY] Have you noticed any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your leg or foot — and if so, in which specific areas (e.g., top of foot, big toe, outer calf)?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I haven’t noticed any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my leg or foot.

[THOUGHT] The absence of sensory or motor deficits is reassuring against severe nerve compression or cauda equina syndrome, but radicular pain alone can still indicate an acute disc herniation — especially with sudden onset during physical exertion. Next, I need to assess for red flags: bowel/bladder dysfunction (e.g., urinary retention, incontinence, constipation), saddle anesthesia (numbness in perineal/genital area), or bilateral leg symptoms — all of which would mandate urgent imaging and neurosurgical evaluation. Since these were not volunteered, I must explicitly ask. Also, history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or cancer could suggest alternative etiologies (e.g., infection, metastasis), but those are less likely given the acute mechanical onset. Prioritize ruling out cauda equina first.

[QUERY] Have you experienced any difficulty urinating, loss of bladder or bowel control, or numbness in your groin or buttock area (like sitting on a saddle)?

[REFERENCE] 12  
[RESPONSE] No, I deny changes in bowel or bladder function.

[THOUGHT] The absence of bowel/bladder dysfunction or saddle anesthesia makes cauda equina syndrome highly unlikely. The presentation remains consistent with acute lumbar radiculopathy, most commonly from a disc herniation. To further support this and assess functional impact, I should evaluate provoking/aggravating factors (e.g., Valsalva maneuvers, sitting, coughing) and relieving factors — classic for disc-related pain. Also, checking for straight leg raise (SLR) sign is a high-yield physical test: a positive SLR (pain radiating below the knee at 30–70°) has good sensitivity for L4–S1 radiculopathy. Since I cannot perform the exam remotely, I’ll ask the patient to self-assess SLR — a validated screening maneuver patients can reliably report.

[QUERY] While lying flat on your back, if you slowly lift one leg straight up (keeping the knee extended), does it reproduce your leg pain — especially radiating down the back or side of the leg — before reaching 70 degrees? Try it gently with each leg separately.

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure — I haven’t tried that specific test, and I don’t recall whether it reproduces the pain.

[THOUGHT] The patient is unable to self-report the straight leg raise (SLR) result, which is a key physical exam finding. Since SLR is highly sensitive for lumbar radiculopathy and can be rapidly assessed in-clinic, I should request it as a targeted physical examination — not a lab test — to avoid diagnostic delay. Performing SLR now will help confirm nerve root irritation and support the clinical diagnosis. No other test at this stage adds more value: imaging (e.g., MRI) is typically reserved for refractory or progressive cases, and labs are low-yield without systemic symptoms. So the next best step is to elicit the SLR sign via direct clinical assessment.

[TEST] Straight leg raise test (bilateral).

[THOUGHT] A positive straight leg raise test — especially with radicular pain radiating below the knee — strongly supports L4–S1 nerve root compression, most commonly due to an acute lumbar disc herniation. The sudden onset during exercise, lateral leg/foot radiation, and absence of red flags (no bowel/bladder dysfunction, no saddle anesthesia, no weakness/numbness) further align with this diagnosis. While other causes (e.g., spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, or tumor) are possible, they typically present more insidiously or with additional features not reported here. Given the classic triad — acute mechanical onset, radicular distribution, and positive SLR — and no contradictory findings, the pretest probability for lumbar disc herniation is very high. No further history or exam is needed to reach a confident clinical diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Lumbar disc herniation
